The proof consists of checking that the "in particular" clause of the proved lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/e624ba applies to $(X,\ell,L)$, namely that $\ell/2$ is not the image in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$ of any class of $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$. That lemma then gives directly that $r$ is even. (The twisted-Hodge hypothesis on $v$ is not needed; it is a redundant assumption.)

Step 1: a slice map. Choose a point $e_0\in E$ and let $i:S\hookrightarrow X$, $i(s)=(s,e_0)$, be the corresponding section of $p$. Then $p\circ i=\mathrm{id}_S$, and $q\circ i$ is the constant map with value $e_0$. By functoriality of pullback,
$$i^{*}\ell=i^{*}p^{*}\lambda+i^{*}q^{*}(m\eta)=(p\circ i)^{*}\lambda+(q\circ i)^{*}(m\eta)=\lambda+0=\lambda,$$
where the last term vanishes because $(q\circ i)^{*}$ factors as $H^2(E,\mathbb Z)\to H^2(\{e_0\},\mathbb Z)\to H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$ and $H^2(\{e_0\},\mathbb Z)=0$. The same computation holds with rational coefficients.

Step 2: $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$ is torsion-free, hence injects into $H^2(S,\mathbb Q)$. A K3 surface is simply connected, so $H_1(S,\mathbb Z)=0$. The universal coefficient theorem for cohomology gives a short exact sequence
$$0\to \operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}(H_1(S,\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)\to H^2(S,\mathbb Z)\to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_2(S,\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)\to 0.$$
The $\operatorname{Ext}$ term vanishes since $H_1(S,\mathbb Z)=0$, and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_2(S,\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)$ is a free abelian group, hence torsion-free. Therefore $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$ is torsion-free, and since $\mathbb Q$ is flat over $\mathbb Z$ (and $H^2(S,\mathbb Q)\cong H^2(S,\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb Q$), the natural map $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)\to H^2(S,\mathbb Q)$ is injective.

Step 3: $\ell/2$ is not an integral class. Suppose, for a contradiction, that there were $c\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ whose image in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$ equals $\ell/2$; equivalently $2c=\ell$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$. Applying $i^{*}:H^2(X,\mathbb Q)\to H^2(S,\mathbb Q)$ and using Step 1 we obtain
$$2\, i^{*}c=\lambda\qquad\text{in }H^2(S,\mathbb Q),$$
with $i^{*}c\in H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$. By the injectivity established in Step 2, the equality holds already in $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$, so $\lambda=2(i^{*}c)\in 2H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$, contradicting the hypothesis $\lambda\notin 2H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$. Hence no such $c$ exists: $\ell/2$ does not lie in the image of $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$.

Step 4: conclusion. We now apply the proved lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/e624ba to the variety $X$, the class $\ell$, the line bundle $L$ (with $c_1(L)=\ell$) and the class $v$ of rank $r$ satisfying $D_\ell(v)=[L]v^{\vee}=v$. That lemma yields $2c_1(v)=r\ell$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$, and its "in particular" clause states that if $\ell/2$ is not the image of a class of $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$ then $r$ is even. Step 3 supplies exactly this hypothesis, so $r=\operatorname{rk}(v)$ is even.

(For completeness we spell out the mechanism inside that lemma's "in particular" clause, which is the whole content used here: $2c_1(v)=r\ell$ makes $r\ell$ divisible by $2$ in the lattice $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ viewed inside $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$; if $r$ were odd, writing $r=2s+1$ and $r\ell=2a$ with $a$ in the image of $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ gives $\ell=2(a-s\ell)$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$, i.e. $\ell/2$ is integral, contradicting Step 3.)

Thus $\operatorname{rk}(v)$ is even, as required.

statement: Let $S$ be a smooth projective complex K3 surface, $E$ an elliptic curve with projections $p,q$ and $\eta$ a generator of $H^2(E,\mathbb{Z})$. For $\lambda\in H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})$ and $m\in\mathbb{Z}$, there exists a class $a\in H^2(S\times E,\mathbb{Z})$ such that $p^*\lambda+q^*(m\eta)=2a$ in $H^2(S\times E,\mathbb{Q})$ if and only if there exists a class $b\in H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})$ such that $\lambda=2b$ in $H^2(S,\mathbb{Q})$ and $m$ is even.
proof:
Let X = S × E, with p: X → S and q: X → E the projections, and let η ∈ H^2(E, Z) be a generator.

STEP 0. Preliminaries on the cohomology groups involved.

(0a) E is a (smooth projective) elliptic curve, hence E ≅ C/Λ is a real 2-torus; in particular H^2(E, Z) ≅ Z, and the given generator η is a Z-basis of H^2(E, Z) (up to sign). In particular H^2(E, Z) is torsion-free, so the natural map H^2(E, Z) → H^2(E, Q) (given by x ↦ x ⊗ 1, injective for any finitely generated abelian group with no 2-... more precisely with no torsion prime-to-nothing: the kernel of H^2(E,Z) → H^2(E,Q) = H^2(E,Z) ⊗ Q is exactly the torsion subgroup) is injective; thus η ≠ 0 in H^2(E, Q) and the elements c·η (c ∈ Z) are pairwise distinct in H^2(E, Q).

(0b) S is a smooth projective complex K3 surface. Such a surface is simply connected (classical theorem on K3 surfaces), hence H_1(S, Z) = 0. The universal coefficient theorem gives a short exact sequence 0 → Ext^1(H_1(S,Z), Z) → H^2(S, Z) → Hom(H_2(S,Z), Z) → 0; the first term vanishes, so H^2(S, Z) ≅ Hom(H_2(S, Z), Z) is a free abelian group. Consequently H^2(S, Z) is torsion-free and the map H^2(S, Z) → H^2(S, Q) is injective. (We will use only torsion-freeness/injectivity, not the identification with the K3 lattice Z^{22}.)

(0c) For any space Y, the pullback along a constant map Y → Z factors as Y → pt → Z, so it is zero on H^i for i > 0, since H^i(pt; Q) = H^i(pt; Z) = 0 for i > 0. Pullback is functorial ((f∘g)^* = g^*∘f^*) and Q-linear after extending scalars.

STEP 1. Choice of sections (slices).
Fix points s_0 ∈ S and e_0 ∈ E and define
   σ: S → X,  s ↦ (s, e_0),      τ: E → X,  e ↦ (s_0, e).
Then p ∘ σ = id_S and q ∘ σ = const_{e_0}; also p ∘ τ = const_{s_0} and q ∘ τ = id_E. Hence by (0c)
   σ^* p^* = id on H^2(S, –),   σ^* q^* = 0 on H^2(E, –),
   τ^* q^* = id on H^2(E, –),   τ^* p^* = 0 on H^2(S, –).        (1)
(Explicitly: σ^*(p^* u) = (p∘σ)^* u = u, and σ^*(q^* w) = (q∘σ)^* w = 0 since w has positive degree.)

STEP 2. Proof of the "only if" direction.
Assume there is a ∈ H^2(X, Z) with
   p^* λ + q^*(m η) = 2a   in H^2(X, Q).      (2)
Apply σ^* to (2). Using (1), the left-hand side becomes λ (viewed in H^2(S, Q)) and the right-hand side becomes 2σ^*(a). Setting b := σ^*(a) ∈ H^2(S, Z), we obtain
   λ = 2b   in H^2(S, Q),
which is exactly the required conclusion about λ (b is an integral class by construction).

Apply τ^* to (2). Using (1), the left-hand side becomes m η (in H^2(E, Q)) and the right-hand side 2τ^*(a). Since H^2(E, Z) = Z·η, there is a unique integer c with τ^*(a) = c η. Substituting gives, in H^2(E, Q),
   m η = 2c η,   i.e.   (m − 2c)·η = 0.
By (0a), η is nonzero in H^2(E, Q) and generates a free rank-one Q-vector space H^2(E, Q) ≅ Q·η, so m − 2c = 0. Hence m = 2c is even.

This proves: existence of a ⇒ (∃ b ∈ H^2(S, Z) with λ = 2b in H^2(S, Q)) and m even. (Note that in fact λ = 2b already holds integrally, by (0b) and injectivity, but we do not need the strengthening.)

STEP 3. Proof of the "if" direction.
Conversely, assume there is b ∈ H^2(S, Z) with λ = 2b in H^2(S, Q), and that m = 2c with c ∈ Z. Define
   a := p^*(b) + c·q^*(η) ∈ H^2(X, Z),
which is an integral class because p^*, q^* preserve integral cohomology and b, η, c are integral. Compute in H^2(X, Q):
   2a = 2p^*(b) + 2c·q^*(η) = p^*(2b) + q^*(2c·η)
where the last two equalities use Q-linearity of p^*, q^* (they come from a homomorphism of abelian groups, hence commute with multiplication by integers). Now p^*(2b) = p^*(λ) because λ = 2b holds in H^2(S, Q) and p^*: H^2(S, Q) → H^2(X, Q) is a well-defined linear map. Also 2c = m as integers, so q^*(2c·η) = q^*(m η) in integral cohomology. Therefore
   2a = p^* λ + q^*(m η)   in H^2(X, Q),
which is the desired conclusion.

STEP 4. Conclusion.
Steps 2 and 3 together give the equivalence stated: p^*λ + q^*(mη) is twice an integral class of H^2(S×E, Z) (up to the equality taken in rational cohomology) if and only if λ is twice an integral class of H^2(S, Z) in rational cohomology and m is even.

Remark (intuition, not used in the proof): by the Künneth theorem and H^1(S, Z) = 0 one has H^2(S×E, Z) = p^*H^2(S, Z) ⊕ q^*H^2(E, Z) as a direct sum of free abelian groups, so divisibility by 2 must be checked on each factor separately; the slice argument of Steps 1–2 is precisely a coordinate-free way of projecting onto the two factors.

No previously proved lemma and no reference from the collection is used; the argument relies only on the listed standard properties of the cohomology of a K3 surface and an elliptic curve (Steps 0a, 0b) and on functoriality of pullback.

statement: Let $S$ be a smooth projective complex K3 surface, $E$ an elliptic curve with projections $p,q$ and $\eta$ a generator of $H^2(E,\mathbb{Z})$. Let $\lambda\in H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})$ satisfy $\lambda\notin2H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})+\operatorname{im}(c_1:\operatorname{Pic}(S)\to H^2(S,\mathbb{Z}))$, let $m\in\mathbb{Z}$, set $X=S\times E$, $\ell=p^*\lambda+q^*(m\eta)$, and let $L$ be a topological complex line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$. Then the positive greatest common divisor of $\{\operatorname{rk}(v): v\in KU^0(X), e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)\in\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X), [L]v^\vee=v\}$ is an even divisor of $4$.
proof:
Let $X=S\times E$ with projections $p:X\to S$, $q:X\to E$, let $\eta$ be a generator of $H^2(E,\mathbb Z)$, let $\lambda\in H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$ satisfy
$$\lambda\notin 2H^2(S,\mathbb Z)+\operatorname{im}\big(c_1:\operatorname{Pic}(S)\to H^2(S,\mathbb Z)\big),\qquad \ell=p^*\lambda+q^*(m\eta)\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z),$$
and let $L$ be a topological complex line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$. Write $D_\ell(u)=[L]u^\vee$. Abbreviate
$$\mathcal S \;=\; \{\operatorname{rk}(v): v\in KU^0(X),\ e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)\in \textstyle\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X),\ D_\ell(v)=v\},$$
so that the lemma asserts that the positive generator $g$ of the ideal $\mathcal I\subseteq\mathbb Z$ generated by $\mathcal S$ is an even divisor of $4$. (Since elements of $KU^0$ may have negative or zero rank, $\mathcal S$ is a set of integers, not of positive integers; $g$ is defined as the positive generator of $\mathcal I$, which is well defined once we know $\mathcal S\neq\varnothing$ and $\mathcal S\neq\{0\}$.)

**Step 0. Two immediate consequences of the hypothesis on $\lambda$.**
Since $\mathcal O_S\in\operatorname{Pic}(S)$ has $c_1(\mathcal O_S)=0$, the subspace $\operatorname{im}(c_1)$ contains $0$, hence $2H^2(S,\mathbb Z)\subseteq 2H^2(S,\mathbb Z)+\operatorname{im}(c_1)$. The displayed hypothesis therefore implies
$$\lambda\notin 2H^2(S,\mathbb Z).\tag{0.1}$$
Also, a K3 surface is simply connected, so $H_1(S,\mathbb Z)=0$; by the universal coefficient theorem $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(H_2(S,\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)$ is a free abelian group (of rank $22$). Hence the natural map $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)\to H^2(S,\mathbb Q)$ is injective, and for integral classes equality in rational cohomology is the same as equality in integral cohomology.

**Step 1. Non-divisibility of $\ell/2$.** We claim
$$\text{there is no } a\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z) \text{ whose image in } H^2(X,\mathbb Q) \text{ equals } \ell/2.\tag{$\ast$}
$$
*Künneth decomposition.* Since $H^1(S,\mathbb Z)=0$ and $H^3(S,\mathbb Z)=0$ (K3 surface) and $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$ is free, the cohomological Künneth short exact sequence for $n=2$,
$$0\to\bigoplus_{r+s=2}H^r(S,\mathbb Z)\otimes H^s(E,\mathbb Z)\to H^2(S\times E,\mathbb Z)\to\bigoplus_{r+s=3}\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathbb Z}(H^r(S,\mathbb Z),H^s(E,\mathbb Z))\to 0,$$
has vanishing right-hand term: the summands are $\operatorname{Tor}(H^2(S),H^1(E))=0$ (because $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$ is free), $\operatorname{Tor}(H^1(S),H^2(E))=0$ (because $H^1(S)=0$) and $\operatorname{Tor}(H^3(S),H^0(E))=0$ (because $H^3(S)=0$). The left-hand term is $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)\oplus H^2(E,\mathbb Z)$, and the isomorphism sends $(a_S,a_E)$ to $p^*a_S+q^*a_E$. Thus every $a\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ is uniquely $a=p^*a_S+q^*a_E$ with $a_S\in H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$, $a_E\in H^2(E,\mathbb Z)$. Tensoring with $\mathbb Q$ gives the analogous statement rationally.

*Conclusion.* If $2a=\ell$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$ with $a=p^*a_S+q^*a_E$ as above, uniqueness in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)\cong H^2(S,\mathbb Q)\oplus H^2(E,\mathbb Q)$ gives $2a_S=\lambda$ in $H^2(S,\mathbb Q)$, i.e. $\lambda=2a_S$ in $H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$ by the injectivity noted in Step 0, contradicting (0.1). This proves $(\ast)$. (No condition on $m$ is used, and none is needed.)

**Step 2. Every element of $\mathcal S$ is even.** Let $v\in\mathcal S$ have rank $r$. By definition $D_\ell(v)=v$, and $c_1(L)=\ell$. We may therefore apply lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/e624ba to $X$, $\ell$, $L$ and $v$: it gives $2c_1(v)=r\ell$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$, and moreover asserts that if $\ell/2$ is not the image of an integral class, then $r$ is even. That is exactly $(\ast)$, so $r\in 2\mathbb Z$. Hence
$$\mathcal S\subseteq 2\mathbb Z.\tag{2.1}$$

**Step 3. The class $v_0$, and $4\in\mathcal S$.** The assignment $c_1$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of topological complex line bundles on $X$ onto $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ (line bundles are classified by maps to $\mathbb CP^\infty$, and $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)\cong[X,K(\mathbb Z,2)]$); hence there is a topological line bundle $B$ on $X$ with $c_1(B)=q^*(m\eta)$. We now invoke lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/d3170e with $\ell_S=\lambda$ and the given integer $m$: its hypotheses (a K3 surface $S$, an elliptic curve $E$, $\ell=p^*\ell_S+q^*(m\eta)$, line bundles $L$, $B$ with these first Chern classes) are precisely ours, and it yields that
$$v_0=[\mathcal O_X]+[L]+[B]+[B^\vee\otimes L]\in KU^0(X)$$
has rank $4$, satisfies $D_\ell(v_0)=v_0$, and lies in $\mathcal H_\ell$, i.e. $e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v_0)\in\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X)$. Thus $v_0$ satisfies all three membership conditions defining $\mathcal S$, so
$$4\in\mathcal S.\tag{3.1}$$
In particular $\mathcal S\neq\varnothing$ and $\mathcal S$ contains a non-zero element, so the ideal $\mathcal I$ it generates is non-zero and $g>0$ is well defined.

**Step 4. Explicit verification of the membership $v_0\in\mathcal H_\ell$ (correct term-by-term computation).** This step is only a check of what Step 3 already supplies via the cited lemma; it is included because it is the computation on which an earlier version went wrong.

Put $x=p^*\lambda$ and $y=q^*(m\eta)$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$, so $\ell=x+y$. Because $S$ is a surface, $\lambda^3\in H^6(S,\mathbb Q)=0$, so $x^3=0$; because $E$ is a curve, $\eta^2=0$, so $y^2=0$. One must nevertheless **not** discard $(x+y)^3=3x^2y$, which lies in $H^6(X,\mathbb Q)$ and need not vanish. Consider the homomorphism of graded rings
$$\varphi:\mathbb Q[\Lambda,M]/(\Lambda^3,M^2)\longrightarrow H^*(X,\mathbb Q),\qquad \Lambda\mapsto x,\ M\mapsto y,$$
which is well defined precisely because $x^3=0$ and $y^2=0$, and is surjective onto the subalgebra generated by $x,y$. Any identity verified in the source ring therefore maps to a valid identity in $H^*(X,\mathbb Q)$; this is why the finite truncated computation below is a proof and not merely a model.

In this ring, using $y^2=0$, $(x+y)^2=x^2+2xy$, $(x+y)^3=3x^2y$:
$$\operatorname{ch}([L])=e^{x+y}=1+x+y+\tfrac{x^2}{2}+xy+\tfrac{x^2y}{2},\quad \operatorname{ch}([B])=e^{y}=1+y,\quad \operatorname{ch}([B^\vee\otimes L])=e^{-y}e^{x+y}=e^{x}=1+x+\tfrac{x^2}{2},$$
hence
$$\operatorname{ch}(v_0)=4+2x+2y+x^2+xy+\tfrac{x^2y}{2}\qquad(\text{of degree }\le 6),$$
and
$$e^{-\ell/2}=e^{-(x+y)/2}=1-\tfrac{x}{2}-\tfrac{y}{2}+\tfrac{x^2}{8}+\tfrac{xy}{4}-\tfrac{(x+y)^3}{48}=1-\tfrac{x}{2}-\tfrac{y}{2}+\tfrac{x^2}{8}+\tfrac{xy}{4}-\tfrac{x^2y}{16}.$$
Multiplying grade by grade (all products of total degree $>6$ vanish, and $x^3=y^2=0$):
\begin{align*}
\text{degree }0:&\quad 4;\\
\text{degree }2:&\quad (2x+2y)-4\tfrac{x+y}{2}=0;\\
\text{degree }4:&\quad (x^2+xy)-(x+y)^2+\big(\tfrac{x^2}{2}+xy\big)=x^2+xy-(x^2+2xy)+\tfrac{x^2}{2}+xy=\tfrac{x^2}{2};\\
\text{degree }6:&\quad \tfrac{x^2y}{2}-\big(\tfrac{x}{2}+\tfrac{y}{2}\big)(x^2+xy)+\big(\tfrac{x^2}{8}+\tfrac{xy}{4}\big)(2x+2y)-4\cdot\tfrac{x^2y}{16}\\
&= \tfrac{x^2y}{2}-x^2y+\tfrac{3x^2y}{4}-\tfrac{x^2y}{4}=0.
\end{align*}
So $e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v_0)=4+\dfrac{x^2}{2}=4+\dfrac{p^*(\lambda^2)}{2}$. The class $\lambda^2\in H^4(S,\mathbb Q)$ is of type $(2,2)$ (as is every class in $H^4$ of a surface), so $p^*(\lambda^2)/2\in H^{2,2}(X,\mathbb Q)$, and therefore $e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v_0)\in H^{0,0}(X)\oplus H^{2,2}(X)\subset\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X)$, as required.

If one groups the four summands into the two pairs $\{\mathcal O_X,L\}$ and $\{B,B^\vee\otimes L\}$, the **correct** per-pair values are
$$e^{-\ell/2}\big(1+\operatorname{ch}[L]\big)=e^{-(x+y)/2}+e^{(x+y)/2}=2\cosh\!\tfrac{x+y}{2}=2+\frac{(x+y)^2}{4}=2+\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{xy}{2},$$
$$e^{-\ell/2}\big(\operatorname{ch}[B]+\operatorname{ch}[B^\vee\!\otimes L]\big)=e^{-\ell/2}\big[(1+y)+(1+x+\tfrac{x^2}{2})\big]=2+\frac{x^2}{4}-\frac{xy}{2}.$$
These two are **unequal**; the $\pm xy/2$ terms cancel only in the sum, giving $4+x^2/2$. In particular neither pair equals $2\cosh(x/2)\cosh(y/2)=2+x^2/4$, since $2\cosh((x+y)/2)=2+x^2/4+xy/2\neq 2+x^2/4$ (e.g. the pairs $\{1,L\}$ and $\{B,B^\vee\otimes L\}$ differ by $xy$).

The script [code:9b31eb02] carries out exactly this arithmetic with rationals (Python `fractions.Fraction`, no floating point) in $\mathbb Q[\lambda,\mu]/(\lambda^3,\mu^2)$ and asserts: (i) the total $e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v_0)$ equals $4+\lambda^2/2$, with the coefficients of $\lambda,\mu,\lambda\mu,\lambda^2\mu$ all exactly $0$; (ii) the two pair-values are $2+\lambda^2/4+\lambda\mu/2$ and $2+\lambda^2/4-\lambda^2\!/4$-corrected, namely $2+\lambda^2/4-\lambda\mu/2$ (coefficients $+1/2$ and $-1/2$ of $\lambda\mu$); (iii) neither pair equals $2+\lambda^2/4$; (iv) $e^{\ell}\cdot\operatorname{ch}(v_0)^\vee=\operatorname{ch}(v_0)$, i.e. $D_\ell$-invariance at the level of Chern characters; and (v) $e^{-\ell/2}(1+\operatorname{ch}[L])=2+\lambda^2/4+\lambda\mu/2$. Because $\varphi$ above is a surjective ring homomorphism onto the subalgebra generated by $x$ and $y$, each of these identities in the model ring is an identity in $H^*(X,\mathbb Q)$.

(We deliberately draw no further conclusion from (v): the class $\mu\lambda=p^*\lambda\smile q^*(m\eta)$ need not be of type $(1,1)$-squared — for $\lambda$ non-algebraic it has components in $H^{2,0}(S)\otimes H^{1,1}(E)\subset H^{3,1}(X)$ — so no assertion is made here that $2=\operatorname{rk}(1+[L])$ lies in $\mathcal S$, and no specific value of $g$ is claimed.)

**Step 5. $g$ divides $4$ and $2$ divides $g$.** By (3.1), $4\in\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal I=g\mathbb Z$, so $g\mid 4$; in particular $g\in\{1,2,4\}$ and $\mathcal I\neq(0)$, so $g>0$ is well defined. By (2.1), every element of $\mathcal S$ lies in $2\mathbb Z$, hence the ideal $\mathcal I$ they generate is contained in $2\mathbb Z$: $g\mathbb Z=\mathcal I\subseteq 2\mathbb Z$. Thus $g\in 2\mathbb Z$, i.e. $2\mid g$. (Equivalently: every integer linear combination of ranks of $D_\ell$-invariant classes in $\mathcal H_\ell$ is even, so in particular the Bézout generator $g$ is even.)

**Step 6. Conclusion.** $g$ is a positive divisor of $4$ and is even, so $g\in\{2,4\}$. That is exactly the assertion that the positive greatest common divisor of $\{\operatorname{rk}(v): v\in KU^0(X),\ e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)\in\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X),\ [L]v^\vee=v\}$ is an even divisor of $4$. $\blacksquare$

Remark on the role of the two cited lemmas: eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/e624ba is used only through its "in particular" clause, applied via $(\ast)$ of Step 1, to force every rank in $\mathcal S$ to be even; eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/d3170e is used to produce an element of rank $4$ in $\mathcal S$ (Step 3), whose existence is also verified by the explicit computation of Step 4. Nothing else is assumed beyond the stated hypotheses on $S$, $E$, $\lambda$ and $m$; in particular the argument is uniform in the parity of $m$, and the lemma claims no more than that $g$ is an even divisor of $4$.)

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth connected projective complex variety, $\ell\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, and $L$ a topological complex line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$, where $c_1:KU^0(X)\to H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ is the additive first Chern class obtained from the determinant. If $v\in KU^0(X)$ has rank $r$ and satisfies $[L]v^\vee=v$, then $2c_1(v)=r\ell$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$.
proof:
**Proof.** We write $X$ also for the complex manifold $X(\mathbb C)$ with its classical topology, and $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ for its singular cohomology; $\ell=c_1(L)\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$. The argument is purely formal (it uses only determinant line bundles) and in fact works for any compact space of the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex.

**Step 1. The setting inside $KU^0(X)$.** A smooth connected complex projective variety has triangulable analytification, hence the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex, so $KU^0(X)$ is (by definition) the Grothendieck group of the commutative monoid $Vect(X)$ of isomorphism classes of topological complex vector bundles under $\oplus$; every $u\in KU^0(X)$ is of the form $u=[V]-[W]$ with $V,W\in Vect(X)$.

$X(\mathbb C)$ is connected: a smooth variety is locally irreducible, so its irreducible components are open, and connectedness forces $X$ to be irreducible, whose analytification is path-connected. Hence every bundle has a constant integer rank, and $\operatorname{rk}(u):=\operatorname{rk}V-\operatorname{rk}W$ is independent of the chosen representation (it is the image of $u$ under the ring homomorphism $KU^0(X)\to KU^0(\ast)=\mathbb Z$ given by restriction to a point).

We shall use the standard form of equality in this Grothendieck group: for $A,B,C,D\in Vect(X)$,
$[A]-[B]=[C]-[D]\iff A\oplus D\oplus\underline{\mathbb C}^{N}\cong C\oplus B\oplus\underline{\mathbb C}^{N}$ for some $N\ge 0$. Indeed the general group-completion criterion gives the equivalence with an arbitrary bundle $G$ in place of $\underline{\mathbb C}^{N}$; since $X$ is compact, choosing a hermitian metric on $G$ and a surjection $\underline{\mathbb C}^{N}\twoheadrightarrow G$ exhibits $G\oplus G'\cong\underline{\mathbb C}^{N}$ for the orthogonal complement $G'$, and adding $G'$ to both sides gives the stated form with a trivial bundle.

**Step 2. $c_1$ on virtual bundles is well defined.** Set $c_1([V]-[W]):=c_1(\det V)-c_1(\det W)$, as in the hypothesis ("additive first Chern class obtained from the determinant"). If $[V]-[W]=[V']-[W']$, Step 1 gives $V\oplus W'\oplus\underline{\mathbb C}^{N}\cong V'\oplus W\oplus\underline{\mathbb C}^{N}$. Taking top exterior powers, and using $\det(E\oplus F)=\det E\otimes\det F$ together with $\det\underline{\mathbb C}^{N}\cong\mathcal O_X$, yields an isomorphism of line bundles $\det V\otimes\det W'\cong\det V'\otimes\det W$. Applying Step 3 below (which turns $\otimes$ into $+$) gives $c_1(V)+c_1(W')=c_1(V')+c_1(W)$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, i.e. $c_1(V)-c_1(W)=c_1(V')-c_1(W')$. So $c_1$ is a well-defined function $KU^0(X)\to H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, additive on the nose: $c_1(u_1+u_2)=c_1(u_1)+c_1(u_2)$.

**Step 3. Additivity of $c_1$ for line bundles.** For topological complex line bundles $M,M'$ on $X$ one has $c_1(M\otimes M')=c_1(M)+c_1(M')$; consequently $c_1(\mathcal O_X)=0$, $c_1(M^{\vee})=-c_1(M)$ (because $M\otimes M^{\vee}\cong\mathcal O_X$), and $c_1(N^{\otimes k})=k\,c_1(N)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$, where $N^{\otimes k}$ for $k<0$ means $(N^{\vee})^{\otimes(-k)}$.

*Justification.* Let $\gamma\to\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}$ be the tautological line bundle and $u=c_1(\gamma)$; every line bundle is a pullback $f^{*}\gamma$, uniquely up to homotopy, and $c_1$ is natural. Put $U:=\mathrm{pr}_1^{*}\gamma\otimes\mathrm{pr}_2^{*}\gamma$ on $\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}\times\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}$. By K\"unneth, $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}\times\mathbb{CP}^{\infty},\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z u_1\oplus\mathbb Z u_2$ with $u_i=\mathrm{pr}_i^{*}u$, so $c_1(U)=\alpha u_1+\beta u_2$ with $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Z$. Restrict along $i_1:\mathbb{CP}^{1}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}$ in the first factor and the base point $\ast$ in the second: $i_1^{*}U\cong\gamma_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}\otimes\underline{\mathbb C}\cong\gamma_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}$ (the pullback of any bundle from a point is trivial), so $c_1(i_1^{*}U)=h$, the positive generator with $i_1^{*}u_1=h$, $i_1^{*}u_2=0$; hence $\alpha=1$, and symmetrically $\beta=1$. Thus $c_1(U)=u_1+u_2$. For $M=f^{*}\gamma$, $M'=g^{*}\gamma$ we obtain $c_1(M\otimes M')=c_1((f,g)^{*}U)=(f,g)^{*}(u_1+u_2)=c_1(M)+c_1(M')$.

**Step 4. Three identities for actual bundles.** For $E\in Vect(X)$ write $c_1(E):=c_1(\det E)$.

(a) *Direct sums.* $c_1(E\oplus F)=c_1(E)+c_1(F)$: this is $\det(E\oplus F)=\det E\otimes\det F$ plus Step 3.

(b) *Duals.* If $\operatorname{rk}E=n$, wedging the natural pairing $E\times E^{\vee}\to\mathcal O_X$ gives a perfect pairing $\Lambda^{n}E\times\Lambda^{n}E^{\vee}\to\mathcal O_X$, i.e. an isomorphism $\det(E^{\vee})\cong(\det E)^{-1}$; with Step 3, $c_1(E^{\vee})=-c_1(E)$.

(c) *Tensoring by $L$.* If $\operatorname{rk}E=n$, then $\det(L\otimes E)=\Lambda^{n}(L\otimes E)\cong L^{\otimes n}\otimes\Lambda^{n}E=L^{\otimes n}\otimes\det E$, whence $c_1(L\otimes E)=n\ell+c_1(E)$ by Step 3. *Construction of the isomorphism.* Over an open set where $L$ and $E$ admit local frames $f$ and $b_1,\dots,b_n$, define, for local sections $\xi_i=\sum_j a_{ij}\,(f\otimes b_j)$ of $L\otimes E$,
$\Phi(\xi_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\xi_n):=f^{\otimes n}\otimes\det(a_{ij})\,(b_1\wedge\cdots\wedge b_n)$.
The right side is multilinear and alternating in the $\xi_i$ (the determinant is alternating multilinear in the rows of $(a_{ij})$, and $\xi_i=\xi_j$ makes two rows equal, giving $0$), so $\Phi$ is well defined once it is independent of the frames. Replacing $f$ by $f'=gf$ ($g$ a non-vanishing local function) replaces $a_{ij}$ by $g^{-1}a_{ij}$ and hence $\det(a_{ij})$ by $g^{-n}\det(a_{ij})$, while $f'^{\,\otimes n}=g^{n}f^{\otimes n}$: no change. Replacing $b$ by $b'=Hb$ with $H\in GL_n$ replaces $\det(a_{ij})$ by $\det(a_{ij})\det(H)^{-1}$ and $b_1'\wedge\cdots\wedge b_n'$ by $\det(H)(b_1\wedge\cdots\wedge b_n)$: no change. So the local definitions glue to a global bundle map $\Phi:\Lambda^{n}(L\otimes E)\to L^{\otimes n}\otimes\Lambda^{n}E$, which is an isomorphism on every fibre since it sends the basis element $(f\otimes b_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(f\otimes b_n)$ to the basis element $f^{\otimes n}\otimes(b_1\wedge\cdots\wedge b_n)$.

**Step 5. The two identities on $KU^0(X)$.** Let $u=[V]-[W]$ with $n_1=\operatorname{rk}V$, $n_2=\operatorname{rk}W$.

(i) Since $E\mapsto E^{\vee}$ is a monoid automorphism of $Vect(X)$ ($(E\oplus F)^{\vee}\cong E^{\vee}\oplus F^{\vee}$), $u^{\vee}=[V^{\vee}]-[W^{\vee}]$. Evaluating the definition of $c_1$ on this representation of $u^{\vee}$ and using Step 4(b): $c_1(u^{\vee})=c_1(V^{\vee})-c_1(W^{\vee})=-c_1(V)+c_1(W)=-c_1(u)$. Also $\operatorname{rk}(u^{\vee})=n_1-n_2=\operatorname{rk}(u)$.

(ii) Since $[L]\cdot[V]=[L\otimes V]$ in $KU^0(X)$, $[L]u=[L\otimes V]-[L\otimes W]$; by Step 4(c),
$c_1([L]u)=c_1(L\otimes V)-c_1(L\otimes W)=(n_1\ell+c_1(V))-(n_2\ell+c_1(W))=(\operatorname{rk}u)\,\ell+c_1(u)$.

**Step 6. Conclusion.** Assume $[L]v^{\vee}=v$ in $KU^0(X)$ and $\operatorname{rk}(v)=r$. Then, in $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$,
$c_1(v)=c_1([L]v^{\vee})\stackrel{(ii)}{=}(\operatorname{rk}(v^{\vee}))\,\ell+c_1(v^{\vee})\stackrel{(i)}{=}r\ell-c_1(v)$,
where $\operatorname{rk}(v^{\vee})=\operatorname{rk}(v)=r$. Adding $c_1(v)$ to both sides gives $2c_1(v)=r\ell$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, which is the claim. Note that the equality is integral, not merely rational: no torsion-freeness of $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ nor any projectivity/K\"ahler input was used. (This strengthens the already proved lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/e624ba, which gives the same identity after tensoring with $\mathbb Q$; that lemma is not used here.) $\blacksquare$

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth connected projective complex threefold, $\ell\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, and $L$ a topological complex line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$. For a topological complex line bundle $A$ with $c_1(A)=a$, set $\beta=a-\tfrac12\ell\in H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$. Then $[A]+[A^\vee\otimes L]$ belongs to $\mathcal H_\ell=\{v:e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)\in\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X)\}$ if and only if $\beta^2\in H^{2,2}(X,\mathbb C)$.
proof:
Throughout, write H^*(-) = H^*(-,\mathbb Z) or H^*(-,\mathbb Q) as convenient, and identify a rational class with its image in complex cohomology when discussing Hodge types. Since X is a smooth complex threefold, it is a finite CW-complex of real dimension 6, so H^m(X,\mathbb Q)=0 for m>6; consequently the cohomology ring H^*(X,\mathbb Q) is nilpotent above degree 6 and all exponential series below terminate, with no completion issues. Note also that the projectivity/connectivity hypotheses give the Hodge decomposition H^n(X,\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}(X), and H^{i,i}(X)\subset H^{2i}(X,\mathbb C), with H^{0,0}(X)=H^0(X,\mathbb C)=\mathbb C (X connected and projective, so H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=\mathbb C).

Step 1: the Chern character of v. Let V\to X be the rank-two bundle A\oplus(A^{\vee}\otimes L), so [V]=[A]+[A^{\vee}\otimes L] in KU^0(X). The Chern character ch:KU^0(X)\to H^{even}(X,\mathbb Q) is additive, is a ring homomorphism, and for a topological line bundle M with c_1(M)=m one has ch(M)=e^{m}\in\prod_i H^{2i}(X,\mathbb Q). Applying this to A (with c_1(A)=a) and to A^{\vee}\otimes L (with c_1(A^{\vee}\otimes L)=-a+\ell, since c_1(A^{\vee})=-c_1(A) and c_1 is additive under tensor product) gives
   ch(v)=e^{a}+e^{\ell-a}.      (1)

Step 2: twisting by e^{-\ell/2}. The class \ell/2\in H^2(X,\mathbb Q), so e^{-\ell/2} is defined; products of exponentials of commuting degree-2 classes add exponents. With \beta:=a-\tfrac12\ell\in H^2(X,\mathbb Q),
   e^{-\ell/2}\,e^{a}=e^{a-\ell/2}=e^{\beta},\qquad e^{-\ell/2}\,e^{\ell-a}=e^{\ell/2-a}=e^{-\beta}.
Hence by (1)
   e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)=e^{\beta}+e^{-\beta}.      (2)

Step 3: explicit expansion. Since \beta has cohomological degree 2 it is even, so the graded-commutative algebra it generates is commutative and
   e^{\beta}+e^{-\beta}=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\beta^k}{k!}+\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-\beta)^k}{k!}=2\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{\beta^{2j}}{(2j)!}=2+\beta^2+\frac{\beta^4}{12}+\frac{\beta^6}{360}+\cdots .
Because \beta\in H^2(X,\mathbb Q) and H^8(X,\mathbb Q)=0 on a threefold, \beta^4=0 and every higher even power vanishes a fortiori. Therefore (2) terminates:
   e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)=2+\beta^2\ \in\ H^0(X,\mathbb Q)\oplus H^4(X,\mathbb Q),      (3)
so its homogeneous components are
   (\,\cdot\,)_0=2,\qquad (\,\cdot\,)_2=0,\qquad (\,\cdot\,)_4=\beta^2,\qquad (\,\cdot\,)_6=0.      (4)
For later reference, (3) says in particular that the degree-2i pieces of the twisted character are 2 (i=0), 0 (i=1), \beta^2 (i=2), 0 (i=3), 0 (i\ge4).

These algebraic identities were verified exactly by a symbolic computation: [code:58ae9561] expands both sides of (2) as polynomials in two commuting degree-2 generators a,\ell over \mathbb Q, truncated at total degree 6 (that is, \beta^6), computing e^{a}, e^{\ell-a}, e^{-\ell/2} by their truncated series and multiplying them; it asserts equality with e^{\beta}+e^{-\beta} and also with 2+\beta^2+\beta^4/12+\beta^6/360, and asserts that after truncation to total (a,\ell)-degree \le 3 (the threefold truncation H^{\le 6}) the result is exactly 2+\beta^2, the discrepancy 2+\beta^2+\cdots-(2+\beta^2) first appearing in degree 4, i.e. \beta^4/12, which vanishes on a threefold. The script's assertions all hold (status ok). Since the computation is in the free graded-commutative \mathbb Q-algebra on two degree-2 generators, it is a proof of the identity in the cohomology ring of an arbitrary space.

Step 4: reduction of the Hodge condition to the degree-4 piece. The subgroup \bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X) is graded: H^{i,i}(X)\subset H^{2i}(X,\mathbb C), and the summands lie in distinct cohomological degrees, so an even class w with homogeneous pieces w_{2i} lies in \bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X) if and only if w_{2i}\in H^{i,i}(X) for every i (necessity by uniqueness of the decomposition into homogeneous pieces, sufficiency by taking the sum).

Apply this to w:=e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)=2+\beta^2, using (4):
 - i=0: w_0=2\in\mathbb C\cdot 1=H^0(X,\mathbb C)=H^{0,0}(X). \checkmark (always satisfied)
 - i=1: w_2=0\in H^{1,1}(X). \checkmark (always satisfied)
 - i=2: w_4=\beta^2\in H^4(X,\mathbb C); the condition is precisely \beta^2\in H^{2,2}(X,\mathbb C).
 - i=3: w_6=0\in H^{3,3}(X). \checkmark (always satisfied)
 - i\ge 4: H^{i,i}(X)=0 because i>\dim_{\mathbb C}X, and w has no component there. \checkmark
All conditions except the one with i=2 hold automatically. Hence
   e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)\in\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \beta^2\in H^{2,2}(X,\mathbb C),
which, by the definition \mathcal H_\ell=\{u:e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(u)\in\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X)\}, is exactly the claimed equivalence for v=[A]+[A^{\vee}\otimes L].

Step 5 (explanation of the resulting condition, for context; not needed for the argument). Decomposing the rational class \beta over the Hodge decomposition of H^2(X,\mathbb C) as \beta=\beta_{2,0}+\beta_{1,1}+\beta_{0,2}, the cup product is a morphism of Hodge structures, so the (3,1)-component of \beta^2 is \beta_{2,0}\cup\beta_{1,1}+\beta_{1,1}\cup\beta_{2,0}=2\,\beta_{2,0}\cup\beta_{1,1} (the terms of bidegrees (4,0) and (0,4) are \beta_{2,0}^2 and \beta_{0,2}^2, which vanish because H^{4,0}(X)=H^0(X,\Omega^4_X)=0 on a threefold, as \Omega^4_X=0 for \operatorname{rk}\Omega^1_X=3). Thus the condition of the lemma is equivalent to \beta_{2,0}\cup\beta_{1,1}=0 in H^{3,1}(X,\mathbb C); in particular it holds automatically whenever \beta is of type (1,1) (e.g. whenever both a and \ell are algebraic and c_1(A)=\tfrac12\ell in H^2(X,\mathbb Q)), but the lemma is stated and proved purely in terms of the type of \beta^2.

This completes the proof of the equivalence.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth connected projective complex variety, $\ell\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, and $L$ a topological complex line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$. If $v\in KU^0(X)$ satisfies $[L]v^\vee=v$, then the class $e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)\in H^{\mathrm{even}}(X,\mathbb Q)$ is a sum of components lying in $H^{4k}(X,\mathbb Q)$; equivalently, its projection to $H^{4k+2}(X,\mathbb C)$ vanishes for every $k\ge 0$.
proof:
Let H^{even}=H^{even}(X,Q)=direct sum over i>=0 of H^{2i}(X,Q), a finite direct sum because X is a compact complex variety. Define tau:H^{even}->H^{even} by tau(x)=(-1)^i x for x in H^{2i}(X,Q). If x in H^{2i} and y in H^{2j}, then tau(xy)=(-1)^{i+j}xy=tau(x)tau(y), so tau is an involution of the graded Q-algebra H^{even}. For any y in H^2(X,Q), exp(y)=sum_{n>=0} y^n/n! is a finite sum because positive-degree cohomology classes are nilpotent, and tau(exp(y))=exp(-y). In particular exp(ell) is a unit in H^{even}(X,Q) with inverse exp(-ell), where ell is viewed in H^2(X,Q).

Write the Chern character of v as ch(v)=sum_i ch_i(v) with ch_i(v) in H^{2i}(X,Q). We use the standard defining properties of the Chern character, which follow directly from its Chern-root description. For an actual complex vector bundle E with Chern roots x_j, one has ch(E)=sum_j exp(x_j). Hence E^vee has Chern roots -x_j, so ch(E^vee)=sum_j exp(-x_j)=tau(ch(E)). If L is a line bundle with c1(L)=ell, then ch(L)=exp(ell), and L tensor E has Chern roots ell+x_j; therefore ch(L tensor E)=sum_j exp(ell+x_j)=exp(ell)ch(E). By additivity of ch on KU^0, these identities extend to virtual bundles: if v=[E]-[F], then v^vee=[E^vee]-[F^vee], so ch(v^vee)=tau(ch(v)), and [L]v^vee=(L tensor E^vee)-(L tensor F^vee), so ch([L]v^vee)=exp(ell)tau(ch(v)).

Assume [L]v^vee=v. Applying the Chern character gives ch(v)=exp(ell)tau(ch(v)). Multiplying by exp(-ell) yields tau(ch(v))=exp(-ell)ch(v). Now set alpha=exp(-ell/2)ch(v), where exp(-ell/2)=sum_{n>=0} (-ell/2)^n/n! is a well-defined class in H^{even}(X,Q). Applying tau and using tau(exp(-ell/2))=exp(ell/2), we obtain tau(alpha)=tau(exp(-ell/2))tau(ch(v))=exp(ell/2)exp(-ell)ch(v)=exp(-ell/2)ch(v)=alpha.

Decompose alpha into homogeneous components, alpha=sum_i alpha_i with alpha_i in H^{2i}(X,Q). The equality tau(alpha)=alpha becomes sum_i (-1)^i alpha_i=sum_i alpha_i. Since H^{even} is the direct sum of its homogeneous pieces, each homogeneous component must vanish: ((-1)^i-1)alpha_i=0 for every i. If i is odd, say i=2k+1, then (-1)^i-1=-2, so -2 alpha_i=0. As H^{2i}(X,Q) is a Q-vector space, this implies alpha_i=0. Therefore alpha has no component in degrees H^{2(2k+1)}=H^{4k+2}(X,Q). Its only possible nonzero components lie in degrees H^{2(2k)}=H^{4k}(X,Q).

Finally, tensoring the vanishing alpha_{2k+1}=0 with C gives vanishing of the corresponding component in H^{4k+2}(X,C). Hence the projection of alpha=e^{-ell/2}ch(v) to H^{4k+2}(X,C) is zero for every k>=0, equivalently alpha is a sum of components lying in H^{4k}(X,Q). This proves the lemma.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth connected projective complex variety, $\ell\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, and $L$ a topological complex line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$. Let $v\in KU^0(X)$ have rank $r$, satisfy $[L]v^\vee=v$ and $e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)\in\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X)$, and let $\operatorname{ch}_2(v)\in H^4(X,\mathbb Q)$ be its degree-four Chern character component. Then $8\operatorname{ch}_2(v)-r\ell^2$ lies in $H^4(X,\mathbb Z)$ and is of type $(2,2)$.
proof: Proof. Write ch(v)=r+ch_1(v)+ch_2(v)+... in H^even(X,Q), where ch_i(v) in H^{2i}(X,Q), and all products are cup products of even-degree classes. Choose topological complex vector bundles E and F with v=[E]-[F] in KU^0(X). Set a=c_1(E), b=c_1(F), A=c_2(E), B=c_2(F), so a,b in H^2(X,Z) and A,B in H^4(X,Z). For the virtual K-class define c_1(v)=a-b and c_2(v)=A-ab+b^2-B. These are the degree-two and degree-four parts of c(E)c(F)^{-1}, hence integral; they are independent of the chosen representative because equality in the Grothendieck group gives stable isomorphism of E⊕F' and E'⊕F, and therefore equality of the corresponding quotients of total Chern classes. Also ch_1(v)=c_1(v). For an actual vector bundle W, the splitting principle gives 2ch_2(W)=c_1(W)^2-2c_2(W). Hence, by additivity of ch, 2ch_2(v)=2ch_2(E)-2ch_2(F)=(a^2-2A)-(b^2-2B)=(a-b)^2-2(A-ab+b^2-B)=c_1(v)^2-2c_2(v). Multiplying by 4 gives 8ch_2(v)=4c_1(v)^2-8c_2(v). The hypothesis [L]v^{vee}=v and the proved lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/e624ba imply 2c_1(v)=r ell in H^2(X,Q). Squaring gives 4c_1(v)^2=r^2 ell^2 in H^4(X,Q). Substitute to obtain 8ch_2(v)-r ell^2=r^2 ell^2-8c_2(v)-r ell^2=r(r-1)ell^2-8c_2(v) in H^4(X,Q). Since ell is integral, ell^2 is integral, and c_2(v) is integral, the right-hand side is the image of a class in H^4(X,Z); this proves integrality. For Hodge type, set w=e^{-ell/2}ch(v). Its degree-four component is w_4=ch_2(v)-(1/2)ell ch_1(v)+(r/8)ell^2. The assumption w in the sum of H^{i,i} and the compatibility of the Hodge decomposition with cohomological grading imply w_4 is of type (2,2). Using ch_1(v)=c_1(v) and 2c_1(v)=r ell, we get ell ch_1(v)=(r/2)ell^2 in H^4(X,Q). Therefore 8w_4=8ch_2(v)-4ell ch_1(v)+r ell^2=8ch_2(v)-2r ell^2+r ell^2=8ch_2(v)-r ell^2. Thus the same class is of type (2,2). Combining integrality and type gives the lemma.

statement: Let X be a smooth connected projective complex variety, and let L,A,B be topological complex line bundles on X with c_1(L)=c_1(A)+c_1(B). Then in KU^0(X), [L]([A]+[B])^\vee=[A]+[B].
proof: We prove the equality in KU^0(X), where addition is direct sum and multiplication is tensor product. Since X is a smooth projective complex variety, it is a compact smooth real manifold, hence paracompact. We first record the classification of topological complex line bundles. A line bundle E has unitary transition functions g_ij: U_i∩U_j → S^1 for some open cover, and isomorphism classes of line bundles are H^1(X,C_{S^1}), where C_{S^1} is the sheaf of continuous S^1-valued functions. The group operation on this H^1 corresponds to tensor product of line bundles, because the transition functions of E⊗F are g_ij(E)g_ij(F). Consider the exponential exact sequence of sheaves 0 → Z → C_R → C_{S^1} → 0, with Z the constant sheaf of integers and C_R the sheaf of continuous real-valued functions. The sheaf C_R is fine, since X is paracompact, so H^q(X,C_R)=0 for q>0. Hence the connecting homomorphism H^1(X,C_{S^1}) → H^2(X,Z) is an isomorphism. Explicitly, choosing local lifts θ_ij in R with exp(2π i θ_ij)=g_ij, the integer cocycle n_ijk=θ_ij+θ_jk−θ_ik represents this connecting homomorphism, and it is precisely the usual first Chern class c_1(E). Therefore two topological complex line bundles are isomorphic if and only if their first Chern classes in H^2(X,Z) are equal. Now c_1(A⊗B)=c_1(A)+c_1(B). Indeed, if a_ij and b_ij are transition functions for A and B, then a_ij b_ij are transition functions for A⊗B, and under the above identification H^1(X,C_{S^1})≅H^2(X,Z), multiplication of S^1-valued cocycles corresponds to addition of their classes. By hypothesis c_1(L)=c_1(A)+c_1(B), so L and A⊗B have the same first Chern class and are therefore isomorphic: L ≅ A⊗B. Next, for any line bundle E, E^∨ has transition functions a_ij^{-1}, so E⊗E^∨ has transition functions 1 and is trivial. Also, for vector bundles V and W, (V⊕W)^∨≅V^∨⊕W^∨. Hence ([A]+[B])^∨ = [A⊕B]^∨ = [A^∨⊕B^∨]. Using the ring structure of KU^0(X), [L]([A]+[B])^∨ = [L] [A^∨⊕B^∨] = [L⊗(A^∨⊕B^∨)] = [(L⊗A^∨)⊕(L⊗B^∨)]. Substituting L ≅ A⊗B gives [(A⊗B)⊗A^∨]⊕[(A⊗B)⊗B^∨] = [B⊗(A⊗A^∨)]⊕[A⊗(B⊗B^∨)] = [B]⊕[A]. In KU^0(X), [B]⊕[A]=[B]+[A]=[A]+[B], since addition is commutative. Thus [L]([A]+[B])^∨ = [A]+[B] in KU^0(X).

statement: Let S be a smooth projective complex K3 surface, E an elliptic curve with projections p,q and \eta a generator of H^2(E,\mathbb Z), and let \lambda\in H^2(S,\mathbb Z) satisfy \lambda^2/4\in H^4(S,\mathbb Z). Set X=S\times E, \ell=p^*\lambda+2q^*\eta, and let A,B be topological complex line bundles with c_1(A)=p^*\lambda+q^*\eta and c_1(B)=q^*\eta. Then in H^*(X,\mathbb Q), e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}([A]+[B])=2+p^*(\lambda^2/4).
proof: Proof. Let u=p^*lambda and v=q^*eta be the corresponding classes in H^*(X,Q), where X=S x E and p,q are the two projections. By the hypotheses on A,B,L, we have c1(A)=u+v, c1(B)=v, and ell=u+2v. Since S is a complex surface, H^6(S,Q)=0, so lambda^3=0; because p^* is a ring homomorphism, u^3=p^*(lambda^3)=0. Since E is a complex curve, H^4(E,Q)=0, so eta^2=0; because q^* is a ring homomorphism, v^2=q^*(eta^2)=0. Thus u and v are nilpotent degree-two elements of the graded-commutative Q-algebra H^*(X,Q). For a topological complex line bundle M, the Chern character is ch([M])=exp(c1(M)) in H^*(X,Q). The Chern character is additive on direct sums, and [A]+[B] is represented by A oplus B, hence ch([A]+[B])=exp(u+v)+exp(v). For commuting nilpotent elements in a Q-algebra, exp(x+y)=exp(x)exp(y); equivalently exp(x)^{-1}=exp(-x). Therefore, in H^*(X,Q), exp(-ell/2)ch([A]+[B]) = exp(-(u+2v)/2)(exp(u+v)+exp(v)) = exp(-u/2-v)exp(u+v)+exp(-u/2-v)exp(v) = exp((-u/2-v)+(u+v))+exp((-u/2-v)+v) = exp(u/2)+exp(-u/2). Since u^3=0, the exponential series terminates: exp(u/2)=1+u/2+u^2/8 and exp(-u/2)=1-u/2+u^2/8. Adding gives exp(u/2)+exp(-u/2)=2+u^2/4. Finally, u^2/4=(p^*lambda)^2/4=p^*(lambda^2/4). Hence exp(-ell/2)ch([A]+[B])=2+p^*(lambda^2/4) in H^*(X,Q). The assumption lambda^2/4 in H^4(S,Z) ensures that the right-hand side is an integral cohomology class pulled back to X, although the equality itself is in rational cohomology.

statement: Let S be a smooth projective complex K3 surface, E an elliptic curve with projections p,q and \eta a generator of H^2(E,\mathbb Z). Let \lambda\in H^2(S,\mathbb Z) satisfy \lambda^2/4\in H^4(S,\mathbb Z) and \lambda\notin 2H^2(S,\mathbb Z)+\operatorname{NS}(S). Set X=S\times E, \ell=p^*\lambda+2q^*\eta, and let L be a topological complex line bundle with c_1(L)=\ell. Then the positive greatest common divisor of the ranks \operatorname{rk}(v) of all v\in KU^0(X) such that [L]v^\vee=v and e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)\in\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X) is equal to 2.
proof:
Let T = { rk(v) : v ∈ KU^0(X), [L]v∨ = v, exp(-ℓ/2)ch(v) ∈ ⊕_i H^{i,i}(X) }. We prove that every element of T is even and that 2 ∈ T.

1. Every rank is even. A K3 surface satisfies H^1(S,Z)=0. By the Künneth theorem, H^2(X,Z) ≅ p^*H^2(S,Z) ⊕ q^*H^2(E,Z) = p^*H^2(S,Z) ⊕ Z q^*η. In H^2(X,Q), we have ℓ/2 = p^*(λ/2) + q^*η. If ℓ/2 were the image of an integral class, then comparing Künneth components would force λ/2 ∈ H^2(S,Z), hence λ ∈ 2H^2(S,Z), contradicting the hypothesis λ ∉ 2H^2(S,Z) + NS(S). Therefore ℓ/2 is not integral.
Now take any v ∈ KU^0(X) with [L]v∨ = v and rank r. Lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/e624ba gives 2c_1(v)=rℓ in H^2(X,Q), and its particular consequence says that r is even under exactly the non-divisibility condition just proved. Hence every element of T is divisible by 2.

2. A rank-two class satisfying the conditions. Let A be a topological complex line bundle with c_1(A)=a=q^*η; such an A exists because integral classes in H^2(X,Z) are first Chern classes of topological line bundles. Define u=[A]+[A∨⊗L]. Then rk(u)=1+1=2.
The self-duality condition holds: D_ℓ([A])=[L]⊗[A∨]=[A∨⊗L] and D_ℓ([A∨⊗L])=[L]⊗[A⊗L∨]=[A], so D_ℓ(u)=u.
It remains to check u ∈ ℋ_ℓ. Apply Lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/eb70d4 to the smooth projective threefold X=S×E. With β=a−ℓ/2=q^*η−(p^*(λ/2)+q^*η)=−p^*(λ/2), the lemma says that [A]+[A∨⊗L] belongs to ℋ_ℓ if and only if β^2 is of type (2,2). But β^2=p^*(λ^2/4). By assumption λ^2/4∈H^4(S,Z). Since S is a complex surface, H^4(S,C)=H^{2,2}(S,C); pullback by the holomorphic map p preserves Hodge bidegree. Therefore β^2∈H^{2,2}(X,C), and the lemma gives u∈ℋ_ℓ.
For clarity, one can also compute directly that exp(-ℓ/2)ch(u)=exp(a-ℓ/2)+exp(ℓ/2-a)=exp(-p^*(λ/2))+exp(p^*(λ/2))=2+p^*(λ^2/4), since (p^*(λ/2))^3=0. This lies in H^{0,0}(X)⊕H^{2,2}(X), and the integral class λ^2/4∈H^4(S,Z) guarantees integrality of the H^4-term if that is part of the convention for H^{i,i}(X).
Thus 2∈T. Since T⊂2Z and contains 2, the positive greatest common divisor of T is exactly 2.

statement: Let S be a smooth projective complex K3 surface, E an elliptic curve with projections p,q and η∈H^2(E,ℤ), and let λ∈H^2(S,ℤ), d∈H^4(S,ℤ) satisfy d=λ^2/4. Let U be a topological complex rank-2 bundle on S with c_1(U)=λ and c_2(U)=d, and let M be a topological complex line bundle on E with c_1(M)=η. Then c_2(q^*M⊗p^*U)=c_1(q^*M⊗p^*U)^2/4 in H^4(S×E,ℚ).
proof:
Let X = S × E and W = q^*M ⊗ p^*U. Set α = p^*λ ∈ H^2(X; Z), β = q^*η ∈ H^2(X; Z), and δ = p^*d ∈ H^4(X; Z). All products are cup products.

First we record the elementary tensor formula for Chern classes. Let Y be a topological space, let V be a complex rank-two bundle on Y, and let N be a complex line bundle on Y with ν = c_1(N). Then in H^*(Y; Q) one has
  c_1(N ⊗ V) = c_1(V) + 2ν,
  c_2(N ⊗ V) = c_2(V) + ν c_1(V) + ν^2.
To justify this, pull back to a complete flag bundle f:Y' → Y with respect to V. By the splitting principle (equivalently, iterating the projective bundle formula), the pullback V' = f^*V has Chern roots x_1,x_2, i.e. after choosing line-bundle graded pieces for a flag we may compute total Chern classes as if V' were L_1 ⊕ L_2 with x_i = c_1(L_i), and f^*:H^*(Y;Q) → H^*(Y';Q) is injective. By naturality of Chern classes, it is enough to prove the equalities after applying f^*, so we work on Y'. Put N' = f^*N and ν = c_1(N'). Then N' ⊗ V' = (N' ⊗ L_1) ⊕ (N' ⊗ L_2). Since c_1(N' ⊗ L_i) = ν + x_i, the total Chern class is
  c(N' ⊗ V') = (1 + ν + x_1)(1 + ν + x_2)
             = 1 + (x_1 + x_2 + 2ν) + (x_1x_2 + ν(x_1+x_2) + ν^2).
But x_1 + x_2 = c_1(V') and x_1x_2 = c_2(V'). Thus the two displayed formulas hold after pulling back by f; injectivity of f^* on rational cohomology gives them on Y.

Now apply the formula with Y = X, V = p^*U, and N = q^*M. Naturality of Chern classes under pullback gives
  c_1(p^*U) = p^*c_1(U) = α,
  c_2(p^*U) = p^*c_2(U) = δ,
and also c_1(q^*M) = q^*c_1(M) = β. Therefore
  c_1(W) = α + 2β,
  c_2(W) = δ + αβ + β^2.

Finally, since p^* is a cohomology ring homomorphism, α^2 = p^*(λ^2). The hypothesis d = λ^2/4 means in H^4(S;Q) that λ^2 = 4d; pulling back to X gives α^2 = 4δ in H^4(X;Q). Hence
  c_1(W)^2 = (α + 2β)^2
           = α^2 + 4αβ + 4β^2
           = 4δ + 4αβ + 4β^2
           = 4(δ + αβ + β^2)
           = 4c_2(W).
Because H^4(X;Q) is a vector space over Q, we may divide by 4 to obtain
  c_2(W) = c_1(W)^2/4
in H^4(X;Q). Substituting W = q^*M ⊗ p^*U yields exactly
  c_2(q^*M ⊗ p^*U) = c_1(q^*M ⊗ p^*U)^2/4
in H^4(S × E; Q).

statement: Let X be a smooth projective complex threefold and V a topological complex vector bundle of rank 2. If c_2(V)=c_1(V)^2/4 in H^4(X,ℚ), then e^{-c_1(V)/2}ch([V])=2 in H^{even}(X,ℚ).
proof:
Let c = c_1(V) in H^2(X,Q). Since X is a complex threefold, H^m(X,Q)=0 for m>6. Therefore c^4=0. Write ch(V)=sum_{k>=0} ch_k(V) with ch_k(V) in H^{2k}(X,Q). Hence ch_k(V)=0 for k>=4, and only ch_0,ch_1,ch_2,ch_3 can appear.

The universal formulas for the Chern character of a rank-two bundle are ch_0=2, ch_1=c_1, ch_2=(c_1^2-2c_2)/2, ch_3=(c_1^3-3c_1 c_2)/6. To see these, use two formal Chern roots x_1,x_2 with x_1+x_2=c_1 and x_1 x_2=c_2. Then ch_k=(x_1^k+x_2^k)/k!, and Newton identities give x_1^2+x_2^2=c_1^2-2c_2 and x_1^3+x_2^3=c_1^3-3c_1 c_2. These are rational polynomial identities in the Chern classes, hence they hold for every topological complex rank-two vector bundle.

Set c=c_1(V) and c_2=c_2(V). By the hypothesis c_2=c^2/4, we obtain
ch_0=2,
ch_1=c,
ch_2=(c^2-2(c^2/4))/2=c^2/4,
ch_3=(c^3-3c(c^2/4))/6=c^3/24.
Thus ch([V])=ch(V)=2+c+c^2/4+c^3/24 in H^{even}(X,Q).

Also e^{-c/2}=1-c/2+c^2/8-c^3/48, since higher terms have degree at least 8 and vanish. Multiplying by degrees and using c^4=0:
degree 0: 2;
degree 2: 2(-1/2)+1 = -1+1 = 0;
degree 4: 2(1/8)+1(-1/2)+1/4 = 1/4-1/2+1/4 = 0;
degree 6: 2(-1/48)+1(1/8)+(1/4)(-1/2)+1/24 = -1/24+1/8-1/8+1/24 = 0;
degrees above 6: 0.
Therefore every positive-degree component of e^{-c/2}ch([V]) is zero and the degree-zero component is 2. Hence e^{-c_1(V)/2}ch([V])=2 in H^{even}(X,Q). This proves the lemma.

statement: Let S be a smooth projective complex K3 surface, E an elliptic curve with projections p,q and η∈H^2(E,ℤ), and let λ∈H^2(S,ℤ) satisfy λ∉2H^2(S,ℤ)+im(c_1:Pic(S)→H^2(S,ℤ)) and λ^2/4∈H^4(S,ℤ). Set X=S×E and ℓ=p^*λ+2q^*η. For every topological complex line bundle L on X with c_1(L)=ℓ, the set of classes v∈KU^0(X) of rank 2 such that [L]v^∨=v and e^{-ℓ/2}ch(v)∈⊕_i H^{i,i}(X) is nonempty.
proof:
We construct, for each line bundle $L$ with $c_1(L)=\ell$, an explicit rank-two class $v\in KU^0(X)$ with $D_\ell(v)=v$ and $v\in\mathcal H_\ell$. Only the formal ring structure of $KU^0(X)$, of $H^*(X,\mathbb Q)$, and the value of $c_1(L)$ are used, so the conclusion holds for every such $L$; the hypotheses $\lambda\notin 2H^2(S,\mathbb Z)+\operatorname{im}c_1$ and $\lambda^2/4\in H^4(S,\mathbb Z)$ are not needed for this lemma.

STEP 0 (topological line bundles realise every class of $H^2(-,\mathbb Z)$). For a finite CW-complex (in particular a smooth complex variety) the set of isomorphism classes of topological complex line bundles is $[X,\mathbb CP^\infty]$, and the universal first Chern class $c_1\in H^2(\mathbb CP^\infty,\mathbb Z)$ is a polynomial generator, so the map $L\mapsto c_1(L)$ is a bijection $[X,\mathbb CP^\infty]\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ (this is the case $n=1$ of the cellular construction of $\mathbb CP^\infty$ with one cell in each even dimension). Hence, given any $x\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, there exists a topological complex line bundle with $c_1=x$, unique up to isomorphism.

STEP 1 (the class $v$). Write $u:=p^*\lambda\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ and $w:=q^*\eta\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, so that $\ell=u+2w$. By Step 0 choose topological complex line bundles $A$ and $B$ on $X$ with
$$c_1(A)=u+w=p^*\lambda+q^*\eta,\qquad c_1(B)=w=q^*\eta.$$
Note $c_1(A)+c_1(B)=u+2w=\ell=c_1(L)$, where $L$ is any line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$. Set
$$v:=[A]+[B]\in KU^0(X),$$
the class of the rank-two bundle $A\oplus B$. Since $X$ is connected, the rank on $KU^0(X)$ is the component map for the identification $KU^0(X)=[X,\mathbb Z\times BU]$, equivalently the degree-$0$ part of the Chern character; hence $\operatorname{rk}(v)=1+1=2$.

STEP 2 (self-duality). Lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/7b91e0 states: for line bundles $L,A,B$ on a smooth connected projective complex variety with $c_1(L)=c_1(A)+c_1(B)$ one has $[L]([A]+[B])^\vee=[A]+[B]$ in $KU^0(X)$. Our choices satisfy exactly this equality of first Chern classes, so with $D_\ell(z)=[L]z^\vee$ we obtain
$$D_\ell(v)=[L]v^\vee=[L]([A]^\vee+[B]^\vee)=[A]+[B]=v .$$
(Equivalently, $A^\vee\otimes L\simeq B$ and $B^\vee\otimes L\simeq A$ topologically, since line bundles with equal first Chern class are isomorphic by Step 0.)

STEP 3 (a universal exponential identity). Let $R=\mathbb Q[u,w]/(u^3,w^2)$ be the graded $\mathbb Q$-algebra with $|u|=|w|=2$; its basis is $\{1,u,w,u^2,uw,u^2w\}$ and the ideal $I=(u,w)$ satisfies $I^4=0$, so $e^x$ is a well-defined finite sum for $x\in I$. In $R$ we claim
$$e^{-(u+2w)/2}\bigl(e^{u+w}+e^{w}\bigr)=2+\tfrac{u^2}{4}.\tag{$*$}
$$
Computation. Using $u^3=0$, $w^2=0$:
$$(u+w)^2=u^2+2uw,\qquad (u+w)^3=3u^2w,\qquad (u+w)^4=0,$$
so $e^{u+w}=1+u+w+\tfrac{u^2}2+uw+\tfrac{u^2w}2$, and $e^{w}=1+w$. Hence
$$P:=e^{u+w}+e^w=2+u+2w+\tfrac{u^2}2+uw+\tfrac{u^2w}2.$$
Further $e^{-(u/2+w)}=e^{-u/2}e^{-w}=(1-\tfrac u2+\tfrac{u^2}8)(1-w)=1-\tfrac u2+\tfrac{u^2}8-w+\tfrac{uw}2-\tfrac{u^2w}8=:Q$. Multiplying, grouping by the $I$-adic degree:
\begin{itemize}
\item degree $0$: $2\cdot1=2$;
\item degree $1$: $2(-\tfrac u2-w)+(u+2w)\cdot1=(-u-2w)+(u+2w)=0$;
\item degree $2$: $2(\tfrac{u^2}8+\tfrac{uw}2)+(u+2w)(-\tfrac u2-w)+(\tfrac{u^2}2+uw)\cdot1=(\tfrac{u^2}4+uw)+(-\tfrac{u^2}2-2uw)+(\tfrac{u^2}2+uw)=\tfrac{u^2}4$;
\item degree $3$: $2(-\tfrac{u^2w}8)+(u+2w)(\tfrac{u^2}8+\tfrac{uw}2)+(\tfrac{u^2}2+uw)(-\tfrac u2-w)+\tfrac{u^2w}2\cdot1=-\tfrac{u^2w}4+(\tfrac{u^2w}2+\tfrac{u^2w}4)+(-\tfrac{u^2w}2-\tfrac{u^2w}2)+\tfrac{u^2w}2=0$,
\end{itemize}
where in the degree-$2$ and degree-$3$ lines all terms containing $u^3$ or $w^2$ were dropped. Thus $QP=2+u^2/4$, proving $(*)$. The same identity was verified by exact rational arithmetic in the script [code:3181766d], which implements $R$ as the $6$-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space with basis $u^aw^b$ ($0\le a\le2$, $0\le b\le1$), multiplies with the truncation $u^3=0$, $w^2=0$ and degree $>6$, computes the exponentials as finite sums, and asserts $e^{-(u+2w)/2}(e^{u+w}+e^{w})=2+u^2/4$ (as well as the cross-check $e^{u/2}+e^{-u/2}=2+u^2/4$, which is the same identity after the cancellation of the $w$-dependence). Since $(*)$ is an identity in the universal ring $R$, it is valid over $\mathbb Q$ with exact coefficients, so the hand computation and the script agree and no case-by-case analysis of $\eta$ is required.

STEP 4 (specialisation to $X$). The assignment $u\mapsto p^*\lambda$, $w\mapsto q^*\eta$ defines a graded $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism $\varphi:R\to H^*(X,\mathbb Q)$: it is well defined because
$$(p^*\lambda)^3=p^*(\lambda^3)=0\quad(\text{as }H^6(S,\mathbb Q)=0,\ \dim_{\mathbb C}S=2),$$
$$(q^*\eta)^2=q^*(\eta^2)=0\quad(\text{as }H^4(E,\mathbb Q)=0,\ \dim_{\mathbb C}E=1).$$
The Chern character of a line bundle is the exponential of its first Chern class and is additive over direct sums, so with the notation of Step 1,
$$\operatorname{ch}(v)=\operatorname{ch}([A])+\operatorname{ch}([B])=e^{u+w}+e^{w}.$$
Because the exponents involved lie in the nilpotent ideal $I$ (whose image under $\varphi$ is nilpotent in $H^{>0}(X,\mathbb Q)$, $X$ being $3$-dimensional), exponentials are finite sums and commute with $\varphi$. Applying $\varphi$ to $(*)$ therefore gives, in $H^*(X,\mathbb Q)$ and with $\ell=u+2w$,
$$e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)=2+\varphi\!\left(\tfrac{u^2}4\right)=2+p^*\!\left(\tfrac{\lambda^2}4\right).\tag{$**$}$$
(As a consistency check, $H^6(X,\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q\,u^2w\ne0$, and the computation shows the coefficient of $u^2w$ — the degree-six component of $e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)$ — is exactly $0$, as recorded by the script.)

STEP 5 (Hodge type). The constant $2$ lies in $H^{0,0}(X)$. For the second term: $\lambda^2\in H^4(S,\mathbb Z)$ and $H^4(S,\mathbb C)=H^{2,2}(S)$ (a surface has no cohomology in bidegrees other than $(2,2)$ in degree $4$), so $\tfrac{\lambda^2}4\in H^{2,2}(S)$. The projection $p:X=S\times E\to S$ is holomorphic, hence $p^*$ preserves the Hodge decomposition, so $p^*(\lambda^2/4)\in H^{2,2}(X)\cap H^4(X,\mathbb Q)$. By $(**)$,
$$e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)=2+p^*(\lambda^2/4)\in H^{0,0}(X)\oplus H^{2,2}(X)\subset\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X),$$
i.e. $v\in\mathcal H_\ell$. Note in particular that the potentially non-$(2,2)$ class $u$ itself does not occur: the degree-two component of $e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)$ vanishes identically by the cancellation in Step 3.

STEP 6 (conclusion). The class $v=[A]+[B]$ has rank $2$ (Step 1), satisfies $D_\ell(v)=v$ (Step 2) and lies in $\mathcal H_\ell$ (Step 5); hence it belongs to the set whose non-emptiness is asserted. The only point at which $L$ was used is Step 2, through the equality $c_1(A)+c_1(B)=c_1(L)=\ell$, which holds for every choice of $L$ with $c_1(L)=\ell$ (Step 0 makes $c_1$ a bijection on isomorphism classes of line bundles). The argument is independent of the auxiliary choices of $A$ and $B$, since $[A],[B]$ depend only on $c_1(A),c_1(B)$ by Step 0. Therefore, for every topological complex line bundle $L$ on $X$ with $c_1(L)=\ell$, the set
$$\{v\in KU^0(X):\operatorname{rk}(v)=2,\ [L]v^\vee=v,\ e^{-\ell/2}\operatorname{ch}(v)\in\textstyle\bigoplus_i H^{i,i}(X)\}$$
is nonempty. $\qquad\blacksquare$

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth connected projective complex threefold with $H^*(X,\mathbb Z)$ torsion-free, let $\ell\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, and let $L$ be a topological complex line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$. For $v\in KU^0(X)$ of rank $2$ satisfying $[L]v^\vee=v$, the class $v$ lies in $\mathcal H_\ell$ if and only if $\operatorname{ch}_2(v)-\ell^2/4$ lies in $H^4(X,\mathbb Z)$ and is of Hodge type $(2,2)$.
proof:
Let t = e^{-ℓ/2} ch(v). Write the Chern character of v as a sum of its cohomological-degree components ch(v) = ch_0(v) + ch_1(v) + ch_2(v) + ch_3(v), with ch_i(v) in H^{2i}(X,Q). Because X is a complex threefold, all components of cohomological degree larger than 6 are zero. The rank is 2, so ch_0(v)=2 and ch_1(v)=c_1(v).

Since H^*(X,Z) is torsion-free, integral cohomology injects into rational cohomology. Apply the proved lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/860166 to the hypothesis [L]v^∨=v with rank r=2. It yields 2 c_1(v)=2ℓ in H^2(X,Z). Since H^2(X,Z) is torsion-free, we may cancel 2 and obtain c_1(v)=ℓ in H^2(X,Z), and hence also in H^2(X,Q). Put a=ch_2(v), b=ch_3(v), and β=a-ℓ^2/4.

The Chern character is additive, multiplicative under tensor product, and takes duals to alternating signs. Therefore for this rank-2 class

ch(v^∨)=2-c_1(v)+ch_2(v)-ch_3(v)=2-ℓ+a-b.

Also ch([L])=e^ℓ. Since [L]v^∨=v in KU^0(X), applying ch gives

ch(v)=e^ℓ ch(v^∨)

in H^{even}(X,Q). Truncate the right-hand side at cohomological degree 6, using ℓ^4=0 on a threefold. We compute

(1+ℓ+ℓ^2/2+ℓ^3/6)(2-ℓ+a-b)
= 2+ℓ+a-b+ℓ a-ℓ^3/6.

Indeed: the degree-2 term is 2ℓ-ℓ=ℓ; the degree-4 term is 2(ℓ^2/2)-ℓ^2+a=a; and the degree-6 term is 2(ℓ^3/6)-(ℓ^2/2)ℓ+ℓ a-b=ℓ^3/3-ℓ^3/2+ℓ a-b=-ℓ^3/6+ℓ a-b.

On the other hand

ch(v)=2+ℓ+a+b.

Equating the two expressions and comparing degree-6 parts gives

b = -b+ℓ a-ℓ^3/6,

so

b = (ℓ a-ℓ^3/6)/2.    (1)

Now expand the twisted Chern character t=e^{-ℓ/2}ch(v). Again only degrees up to 6 occur, so

e^{-ℓ/2}=1-ℓ/2+ℓ^2/8-ℓ^3/48,

and

t=(1-ℓ/2+ℓ^2/8-ℓ^3/48)(2+ℓ+a+b).

The degree-by-degree calculation is explicit:
- degree 0: 2;
- degree 2: (-ℓ/2)·2+ℓ=-ℓ+ℓ=0;
- degree 4: (ℓ^2/8)·2+(-ℓ/2)·ℓ+a=ℓ^2/4-ℓ^2/2+a=a-ℓ^2/4;
- degree 6: (-ℓ^3/48)·2+(ℓ^2/8)·ℓ+(-ℓ/2)·a+b=-ℓ^3/24+ℓ^3/8-ℓ a/2+b=ℓ^3/12-ℓ a/2+b.

By equation (1), the degree-6 component is zero. Hence, as a rational cohomology class,

t=2+β,

where β=ch_2(v)-ℓ^2/4.

By definition of the integral twisted Hodge subgroup H_ℓ, the class v lies in H_ℓ if and only if t is a sum of integral Hodge classes, i.e. if and only if each graded piece of t lies in H^{2i}(X,Z)∩H^{i,i}(X,C). The equality t=2+β has only a degree-0 summand and a degree-4 summand. The degree-0 summand is 2, which lies in H^0(X,Z)=Z because X is connected, and it is automatically of Hodge type (0,0). Therefore t is a sum of integral Hodge classes if and only if β is an integral class in H^4(X,Z) and is of Hodge type (2,2).

Thus v∈H_ℓ if and only if ch_2(v)-ℓ^2/4 lies in H^4(X,Z) and is of Hodge type (2,2).

statement: Let S be a smooth projective complex K3 surface and let λ∈H^2(S,ℤ) satisfy λ^2/4∈H^4(S,ℤ). There exists a topological complex vector bundle U of rank 2 on S with c_1(U)=λ and c_2(U)=λ^2/4.
proof:
Proof. We first prove the following more general topological existence statement.

Let X be a 4-dimensional CW complex. For every x in H^2(X,Z) and every y in H^4(X,Z), there exists a rank-2 topological complex vector bundle E over X with c1(E)=x and c2(E)=y.

Recall that isomorphism classes of rank-2 topological complex vector bundles over X are classified by homotopy classes of maps X -> BU(2). Let u1 in H^2(BU(2),Z) and u2 in H^4(BU(2),Z) be the universal Chern classes. We will show that the 4-type of BU(2) is K(Z,2) times K(Z,4), and that u1 and u2 give the two factors independently.

Compute the low homotopy groups of BU(2). The action of U(2) on the unit sphere of C^2 gives a fibration U(1) -> U(2) -> S^3. Its long exact homotopy sequence implies pi_2(U(2))=0, pi_3(U(2))=Z, and pi_1(U(2))=Z, because U(1)=S^1. Since pi_i(BG)=pi_{i-1}(G) for a connected topological group G, we obtain
pi_1(BU(2))=0,
pi_2(BU(2))=Z,
pi_3(BU(2))=0,
pi_4(BU(2))=Z.

The universal first Chern class u1 induces an isomorphism on pi_2. Indeed, BU(1)=K(Z,2) maps to BU(2) by L -> L plus a trivial line. Pulling back u1 along this map gives the universal first Chern class on BU(1), hence the fundamental class in H^2(K(Z,2),Z). Since the inclusion U(1) -> U(2) induces an isomorphism pi_1(U(1)) -> pi_1(U(2)), the map BU(1) -> BU(2) is an isomorphism on pi_2. Therefore u1 is the generator corresponding to pi_2(BU(2))=Z.

The universal second Chern class u2 induces an isomorphism on pi_4. Restrict from BU(2) to BSU(2). The determinant fibration SU(2) -> U(2) -> U(1) gives an isomorphism pi_3(SU(2)) -> pi_3(U(2)), and hence an isomorphism pi_4(BSU(2)) -> pi_4(BU(2)). Since SU(2)=S^3, pi_3(SU(2))=Z. Thus pi_4(BSU(2))=Z.

The positive generator of pi_4(BSU(2)) is represented by the Hopf rank-2 complex bundle H over S^4 obtained by clutching the two trivial bundles C^2 x D^4_+ and C^2 x D^4_- by the identity map id:S^3 -> SU(2)=S^3. Its determinant is trivial. For a complex rank-2 bundle, c2 is the Euler class of the underlying oriented real rank-4 bundle. The unit sphere bundle of H is an S^3-bundle over S^4 with the same identity clutching map. The primary obstruction to a nowhere-zero section of H is exactly the homotopy class of this clutching map in pi_3(S^3)=Z. Since the identity represents the generator, the Euler class, hence c2(H), is the positive generator of H^4(S^4,Z). Therefore u2 evaluates on the generator of pi_4(BSU(2)) as 1, and its image in pi_4(BU(2)) also has u2-value 1. Consequently u2 induces an isomorphism pi_4(BU(2)) -> Z.

Now form the map
p: BU(2) -> P := K(Z,2) x K(Z,4)
where the first coordinate is the map classifying u1 and the second coordinate is the map classifying u2. By the previous paragraph, p induces isomorphisms on pi_1, pi_2, pi_3, and pi_4. Replacing p by a Serre fibration, its fiber has no homotopy groups in dimensions 1, 2, and 3. Standard cellular obstruction theory then implies that every map from a 4-dimensional CW complex X to P lifts to a map X -> BU(2). In fact [X,BU(2)] -> [X,P] is bijective, but only surjectivity is needed.

Since [X,K(Z,2)]=H^2(X,Z) and [X,K(Z,4)]=H^4(X,Z), the space of maps X -> P is naturally H^2(X,Z) x H^4(X,Z). Given x in H^2(X,Z) and y in H^4(X,Z), choose g:X -> P corresponding to (x,y), and lift it to f:X -> BU(2). Let E be the rank-2 complex vector bundle classified by f. Then
f^*u1 = x and f^*u2 = y,
because u1 and u2 are, by construction, the pullbacks from the two factors of P. This proves the general existence statement for rank-2 bundles over 4-dimensional CW complexes.

Now apply this to X=S. A smooth projective complex surface is a compact real 4-manifold, hence has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex of dimension 4. The class lambda lies in H^2(S,Z), and by hypothesis lambda^2/4 is an element of H^4(S,Z). Using the general statement with x=lambda and y=lambda^2/4, there exists a rank-2 topological complex vector bundle U on S such that c1(U)=lambda and c2(U)=lambda^2/4.

This is exactly the desired conclusion.

statement: Let $S$ be a smooth projective complex K3 surface, $E$ an elliptic curve with projections $p,q$ and $\eta$ a generator of $H^2(E,\mathbb Z)$. Let $\lambda\in H^2(S,\mathbb Z)$ be orthogonal to $\operatorname{NS}(S)$, have $\lambda^{2,0}\neq0$, satisfy $\int_S\lambda^2$ divisible by $4$, and satisfy $\lambda\notin2H^2(S,\mathbb Z)+\operatorname{NS}(S)$. Set $X=S\times E$, $\ell=p^*\lambda+q^*(2\eta)$, and let $L$ be a topological complex line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$. Then there exists $v\in KU^0(X)$ of rank $2$ such that $[L]v^\vee=v$ and $\operatorname{ch}_2(v)-\ell^2/4$ lies in $H^4(X,\mathbb Z)$ and is of Hodge type $(2,2)$.
proof: Put alpha = p^*lambda and beta = q^*eta in H^2(X,Z), where X = S × E. Then ell = alpha + 2 beta. Since X has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex, topological complex line bundles on X are classified by H^2(X,Z) via the first Chern class: the standard identification [X,BU(1)] ≅ [X,CP^∞] ≅ H^2(X,Z) sends a line bundle to c1. Hence there exist topological complex line bundles B and A on X with c1(B) = beta and c1(A) = alpha + beta. Define v = [A] + [B] in KU^0(X). This is the K-theory class of the rank-2 topological vector bundle A ⊕ B, so rank(v) = 2. We also have c1(A) + c1(B) = (alpha + beta) + beta = alpha + 2 beta = ell = c1(L). Therefore the proved lemma eoinm/f10774f5cc5bee21/7b91e0 applies to L,A,B and gives [L]v^∨ = v. It remains to compute ch_2(v) - ell^2/4. Set a = c1(A) and b = c1(B). For a topological complex line bundle M with c1(M) = x, ch(M) = exp(x); since the Chern character is additive, c1(v) = a + b and ch_2(v) = (a^2 + b^2)/2 in H^4(X,Q). All classes a,b have degree 2, so cup product is commutative. Thus ch_2(v) - ell^2/4 = (a^2 + b^2)/2 - (a + b)^2/4 = (a - b)^2/4. But a - b = (alpha + beta) - beta = alpha = p^*lambda. Consequently ch_2(v) - ell^2/4 = alpha^2/4 = p^*(lambda^2/4) in H^4(X,Q). We now verify that the right-hand side is integral and of Hodge type (2,2). Because S is a K3 surface, H^4(S,Z) is free of rank one and the evaluation map c ↦ ∫_S c is an isomorphism H^4(S,Z) ≅ Z. The hypothesis that ∫_S lambda^2 is divisible by 4 means that the integral class lambda^2 is four times an integral class; hence lambda^2/4 ∈ H^4(S,Z). Pullback p^*: H^4(S,Z) → H^4(X,Z) preserves integrality, so p^*(lambda^2/4) ∈ H^4(X,Z). Finally, for the complex surface S, H^4(S,C) = H^{2,2}(S), since no Hodge summands of total degree 4 other than (2,2) occur. Thus lambda^2/4 has Hodge type (2,2). The projection p: S × E → S is holomorphic, and its cohomological pullback preserves Hodge bidegree, so p^*(lambda^2/4) lies in H^{2,2}(X). Therefore v is a rank-2 class satisfying [L]v^∨ = v and ch_2(v) - ell^2/4 ∈ H^4(X,Z) of type (2,2).

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth connected projective complex variety, $L$ a topological complex line bundle on $X$ with $c_1(L)=\ell$, and for $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$ let $F_\varepsilon:GW^\varepsilon(X;L)\to KU^0(X)$ be the forgetful homomorphism from the Grothendieck group of topological complex vector bundles with nondegenerate $L$-valued $\varepsilon$-symmetric bilinear forms. Then for every $v\in\operatorname{im}(F_{+1})$, the class $2v$ lies in $\operatorname{im}(F_{-1})$.
proof: Proof. Let v be an element of im(F_{+1}). By definition there is an element ξ in GW^{+1}(X;L) with F_{+1}(ξ)=v. Since GW^{+1}(X;L) is the Grothendieck group of the monoid of isomorphism classes of actual nondegenerate L-valued symmetric bilinear forms under orthogonal direct sum, we can write ξ=[A]-[B], where A=(E_A,b_A) and B=(E_B,b_B) are actual symmetric forms, with the zero form allowed. It suffices to show that for every actual symmetric form (E,b) there is an actual alternating L-valued form H(E,b) whose underlying K-theory class is 2[E]. Fix such (E,b). Let E^∨ denote the complex dual bundle and put W=E⊕(E^∨⊗L). For local sections x,y of E and φ,ψ of E^∨⊗L define h((x,φ),(y,ψ))=φ(y)-ψ(x), a local section of L. This gives an L-valued bundle morphism W⊗W→L. It is -1-symmetric because h((y,ψ),(x,φ))=ψ(x)-φ(y)=-h((x,φ),(y,ψ)); in particular h((x,φ),(x,φ))=0. It is nondegenerate: if h((x,φ),(y,ψ))=0 for all (y,ψ), taking ψ=0 gives φ(y)=0 for all y, hence φ=0; then taking φ=0 gives ψ(x)=0 for all ψ, hence x=0. Fiberwise, the adjoint W→W^∨⊗L has zero kernel, and because W has finite rank it is an isomorphism. Hence H(E,b)=(W,h) is a nondegenerate L-valued alternating form, i.e. an element of GW^{-1}(X;L). Because b is nondegenerate, its adjoint β_b:E→E^∨⊗L, β_b(x)(y)=b(x,y), is a vector bundle isomorphism. Thus [E^∨⊗L]=[E] in KU^0(X). Therefore F_{-1}([H(E,b)])=[W]=[E]+[E^∨⊗L]=2[E]=2F_{+1}([E,b]). Applying this to A and B, the element η=[H(A)]-[H(B)] lies in GW^{-1}(X;L), and using that F_{-1} is a homomorphism gives F_{-1}(η)=F_{-1}([H(A)])-F_{-1}([H(B)])=2F_{+1}([A])-2F_{+1}([B])=2F_{+1}([A]-[B])=2v. Hence 2v∈im(F_{-1}). The case of zero or virtual classes is included: the zero form gives the zero alternating form, and a chosen representation of ξ as a difference of forms suffices to produce one preimage in GW^{-1}. QED.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth connected projective complex variety of dimension at most $4$, let $\ell\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ with $L$ a topological complex line bundle satisfying $c_1(L)=\ell$, and let $A,B$ be topological complex line bundles with $c_1(A)=a$, $c_1(B)=b$. Set $\beta_A=a-\tfrac12\ell$ and $\beta_B=b-\tfrac12\ell$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$. Then $v=[A]+[A^\vee\otimes L]+[B]+[B^\vee\otimes L]$ has rank $4$, satisfies $[L]v^\vee=v$ and $v\in\operatorname{im}(F_{+1})$, and $v\in\mathcal H_\ell$ if and only if $\beta_A^{\,2}+\beta_B^{\,2}\in H^{2,2}(X,\mathbb C)$.
proof: Proof. Let W_A = A ⊕ (A^∨ ⊗ L) and W_B = B ⊕ (B^∨ ⊗ L); then v = [W_A] + [W_B]. Because X is connected, the rank homomorphism KU^0(X) -> Z is well defined and additive. Since A and B are line bundles, rank(W_A) = rank(W_B) = 2, and therefore rank(v) = 4. For the involution, use [E]^∨ = [E^{-1}] and tensor products of line bundles. We have v^∨ = [A^∨] + [A ⊗ L^∨] + [B^∨] + [B ⊗ L^∨], hence [L]v^∨ = [L ⊗ A^∨] + [A] + [L ⊗ B^∨] + [B] = [A^∨ ⊗ L] + [A] + [B^∨ ⊗ L] + [B] = v. To see that v lies in im(F_{+1}), construct a symmetric L-valued bilinear form on W_A ⊕ W_B. For any line bundle E on X, define h_E on E ⊕ (E^∨ ⊗ L) by h_E((u,α),(v,β)) = α(v) + β(u), where α and β are local sections of E^∨ ⊗ L and u and v are local sections of E; the terms α(v) and β(u) are local sections of L via the evaluation pairing (E^∨ ⊗ L) ⊗ E -> L. This pairing is symmetric because addition in the fibers of L is commutative. The induced map Φ_E: E ⊕ (E^∨ ⊗ L) -> (E ⊕ (E^∨ ⊗ L))^∨ ⊗ L sends (u,α) to the functional (v,β) ↦ α(v) + β(u). Under the canonical identifications (E ⊕ (E^∨ ⊗ L))^∨ ⊗ L ≅ (E^∨ ⊗ L) ⊕ E and ((E^∨ ⊗ L)^∨ ⊗ L) ≅ E, it is Φ_E(u,α) = (α,u), which is an isomorphism. Hence h_E is nondegenerate. Taking E = A and E = B and forming the orthogonal direct sum gives a nondegenerate symmetric L-valued bilinear form h on W = W_A ⊕ W_B. Thus (W,h) is an object of GW^{+1}(X;L), and its image under the forgetful homomorphism is [W] = [W_A] + [W_B] = v. Now analyze the twisted Chern character. For a topological complex line bundle M with c_1(M) = m, ch([M]) = e^m. Therefore ch(v) = e^a + e^{-a+ℓ} + e^b + e^{-b+ℓ}. Multiplying by e^{-ℓ/2} gives e^{-ℓ/2} ch(v) = e^{β_A} + e^{-β_A} + e^{β_B} + e^{-β_B}, because β_A = a - ℓ/2 and β_B = b - ℓ/2. For a degree-2 class γ ∈ H^2(X,Q), the odd powers in e^γ + e^{-γ} cancel, and the nonzero even terms are 2, γ^2, γ^4/12, γ^6/360, ... . Since X has complex dimension at most 4, H^m(X,Q)=0 for m>8; in particular γ^6 ∈ H^{12}(X,Q)=0 and all higher powers vanish. Hence e^γ + e^{-γ} = 2 + γ^2 + γ^4/12 in H^{even}(X,Q). Applying this with γ = β_A and γ = β_B gives e^{-ℓ/2} ch(v) = 4 + T + U/12, where T = β_A^2 + β_B^2 ∈ H^4(X,Q) and U = β_A^4 + β_B^4 ∈ H^8(X,Q). The class U is automatically of type (4,4). Indeed, by the Hodge decomposition for smooth projective complex varieties, H^8(X,C) = ⊕_{p+q=8} H^{p,q}(X,C), and H^{p,q}(X,C)=0 unless 0 ≤ p,q ≤ dim X ≤ 4. If dim X < 4 then H^8(X,C)=0; if dim X = 4 the only possible pair with p+q=8 and p,q ≤ 4 is (4,4). Thus U/12 has type (4,4). Also the rank term 4 has type (0,0), and there are no components of total degree 2 or 6 because all odd powers canceled. Therefore the only possible non-diagonal component of e^{-ℓ/2} ch(v) is its total-degree-4 component T. If T ∈ H^{2,2}(X,C), then every homogeneous component of e^{-ℓ/2} ch(v) lies in H^{0,0} ⊕ H^{2,2} ⊕ H^{4,4}, so v ∈ H_ℓ. Conversely, if v ∈ H_ℓ, then e^{-ℓ/2} ch(v) lies in ⊕_i H^{i,i}(X). Projecting the equality e^{-ℓ/2} ch(v) = 4 + T + U/12 to total degree 4 gives T, and a diagonal Hodge class of total degree 4 must lie in H^{2,2}(X,C). Hence T ∈ H^{2,2}(X,C). This completes the proof.

statement: Let $S_1,S_2$ be smooth projective complex surfaces with projections $p,q$, let $u\in H^2(S_1,\mathbb Q)$ and $v\in H^2(S_2,\mathbb Q)$ have Hodge components $u^{2,0},u^{1,1},u^{0,2}$ and $v^{2,0},v^{1,1},v^{0,2}$. Then $(p^{*}u+q^{*}v)^2\in H^4(S_1\times S_2,\mathbb Q)$ is of type $(2,2)$ if and only if $u^2$ and $v^2$ are of type $(2,2)$ and $u^{2,0}\wedge v^{2,0}$, $u^{2,0}\wedge v^{1,1}$, $u^{1,1}\wedge v^{2,0}$ all vanish.
proof:
Let X = S1 × S2 with projections p and q. We work after extension of scalars to C. For α ∈ H^*(S1,C) and β ∈ H^*(S2,C), write α ∧ β for p^*α ∪ q^*β ∈ H^*(X,C). By the Künneth formula and the product Hodge decomposition, H^{r,s}(X) = ⊕_{a+c=r, b+d=s} H^{a,b}(S1) ⊗ H^{c,d}(S2), and α ∧ β corresponds to α ⊗ β. Pullback preserves Hodge type, and cup product adds bidegrees.

For a smooth projective surface, nonzero Hodge bidegrees of degree 2 are only (2,0), (1,1), (0,2), and H^4 has only bidegree (2,2). Thus write
u = u^{2,0} + u^{1,1} + u^{0,2},
v = v^{2,0} + v^{1,1} + v^{0,2}.
For brevity put u20 = u^{2,0}, u11 = u^{1,1}, u02 = u^{0,2}, and similarly v20, v11, v02.

Consider
W = (p^*u + q^*v)^2 ∈ H^4(X,Q).
Expanding and using graded commutativity in degree 2,
W = p^*(u^2) + 2 (u ∧ v) + q^*(v^2).
Since S1 and S2 are surfaces, p^*(u^2) lies in H^{2,2}(S1) ⊗ H^{0,0}(S2) ⊂ H^{2,2}(X), and q^*(v^2) lies in H^{0,0}(S1) ⊗ H^{2,2}(S2) ⊂ H^{2,2}(X). Hence these two summands have no non-(2,2) Hodge components. In particular, the condition that u^2 and v^2 be of type (2,2) is automatic for smooth projective surfaces, but it is harmless to keep it as stated.

Now decompose u ∧ v according to bidegrees. Since u and v have degree 2, the only bidegrees appearing in W are (4,0), (3,1), (2,2), (1,3), (0,4). The non-(2,2) parts are:
- H^{4,0}: u20 ∧ v20;
- H^{3,1}: u20 ∧ v11 + u11 ∧ v20;
- H^{1,3}: u11 ∧ v02 + u02 ∧ v11;
- H^{0,4}: u02 ∧ v02.
There is no mixing inside H^{3,1}: the class u20 ∧ v11 lies in the Künneth-Hodge summand H^{2,0}(S1) ⊗ H^{1,1}(S2), while u11 ∧ v20 lies in the distinct summand H^{1,1}(S1) ⊗ H^{2,0}(S2). The same directness holds for H^{1,3}. Because the Hodge decomposition is a direct sum, W has type (2,2) if and only if all four non-(2,2) components above vanish. Since the scalar 2 is invertible over Q and C, this is equivalent to vanishing of the corresponding components of u ∧ v.

First suppose W has type (2,2). Then its H^{4,0}-component vanishes, so u20 ∧ v20 = 0. Its H^{3,1}-component also vanishes, so u20 ∧ v11 + u11 ∧ v20 = 0. By directness of the two Künneth-Hodge summands inside H^{3,1}, both summands must vanish individually, hence u20 ∧ v11 = 0 and u11 ∧ v20 = 0. Finally, u^2 and v^2 are automatically of type (2,2) on a smooth projective surface. Thus the stated conditions hold.

Conversely, suppose u^2 and v^2 are of type (2,2) and
u20 ∧ v20 = 0,
u20 ∧ v11 = 0,
u11 ∧ v20 = 0.
Because u and v are rational classes, complex conjugation fixes them and acts on their Hodge components by
conj(u20) = u02, conj(u11) = u11, conj(v20) = v02, conj(v11) = v11.
Conjugation is compatible with cup product and with pullback to the product. Therefore the three assumed vanishings imply the conjugate vanishings
u02 ∧ v02 = 0,
u02 ∧ v11 = 0,
u11 ∧ v02 = 0.
Hence the H^{0,4}-component u02 ∧ v02 vanishes and the H^{1,3}-component u11 ∧ v02 + u02 ∧ v11 vanishes. The assumed vanishings also give vanishing of the H^{4,0}-component and of both summands of the H^{3,1}-component. The only possibly nonzero Hodge components of W are therefore those of type (2,2): the square terms p^*(u^2), q^*(v^2), and the H^{2,2}-part of 2u ∧ v. Since the Hodge decomposition in degree 4 is direct, W ∈ H^{2,2}(X).

Thus (p^*u + q^*v)^2 is of Hodge type (2,2) exactly when u^2 and v^2 are of type (2,2) and u20 ∧ v20, u20 ∧ v11, u11 ∧ v20 all vanish.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth connected projective complex variety, let $\ell\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, let $L$ be a topological complex line bundle with $c_1(L)=\ell$, and let $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$. Assume every class in the image of $F_\varepsilon$ satisfies $[L]v^\vee=v$. If both sets of ranks defining $d_{\mathrm{sd}}(X,\ell)$ and $d_\varepsilon(X,\ell)$ are nonempty, then $d_{\mathrm{sd}}(X,\ell)$ divides $d_\varepsilon(X,\ell)$.
proof:
Write $D=D_\ell:KU^0(X)\to KU^0(X)$, $D(v)=[L]v^\vee$, and set
$$S_{\mathrm{sd}}=\{\rk(v):v\in\mathcal H_\ell,\ D(v)=v\},\qquad S_{\varepsilon}=\{\rk(v):v\in\mathcal H_\ell\cap\operatorname{im}(F_\varepsilon)\}.$$
By hypothesis both sets are nonempty, and $d_{\mathrm{sd}}(X,\ell)=\gcd(S_{\mathrm{sd}})$, $d_\varepsilon(X,\ell)=\gcd(S_\varepsilon)$, with $\gcd$ of a nonempty set of integers taken to be the non-negative generator of the ideal it spans.

Step 1 (the rank is well defined). Since $X$ is connected and non-empty (smooth projective variety over $\mathbb C$), $K^0(X)=KU^0(X)$ has a well-defined rank homomorphism $\rk:KU^0(X)\to\mathbb Z$, obtained by restricting to a point $x\in X$, i.e. $\rk(v)=\rk(v|_x)$; it is independent of $x$ because $X$ is connected. Thus $S_{\mathrm{sd}},S_\varepsilon$ are well-defined subsets of $\mathbb Z$.

Step 2 (set inclusion). Take any $n\in S_\varepsilon$. By definition $n=\rk(v)$ for some $v\in\mathcal H_\ell\cap\operatorname{im}(F_\varepsilon)$. The class $v$ lies in the image of $F_\varepsilon$, so by the standing assumption of the lemma it satisfies $D(v)=[L]v^\vee=v$. Since also $v\in\mathcal H_\ell$, the same $v$ witnesses $n=\rk(v)\in S_{\mathrm{sd}}$. Hence
$$S_\varepsilon\subseteq S_{\mathrm{sd}}.$$
(Equivalently: $\mathcal H_\ell\cap\operatorname{im}(F_\varepsilon)\subseteq\{v\in\mathcal H_\ell:D(v)=v\}$, because $\operatorname{im}(F_\varepsilon)\subseteq\{v:D(v)=v\}$ by assumption; applying $\rk$ gives the inclusion of the sets of ranks.)

Step 3 (a universal-divisor argument for gcds of sets of integers).
